back: Energy from a source naturally replaced as fast as it is used, so it will not run out.
Energy from a finite source that cannot be replaced within a human timescale.
Hydrogen reacts with oxygen to produce electricity, with water as the only emission at the point of use.
Most hydrogen is currently made from fossil fuels, it is hard to store and transport, and there are very few refuelling stations.
Not a fossil fuel and produces almost no CO₂ in operation, but the fuel is finite and radioactive waste stays dangerous for thousands of years.
Greenhouse gases, air pollution and acid rain, finite and unstable supply, extraction damage and political dependence on imports.
No fuel cost or emissions, can be offshore, quick to build — but only works when windy, visually intrusive, noise and risk to birds.
Free energy once installed, little maintenance, any scale — but expensive to install, nothing at night, needs a large area for large output.
Constant output day and night with a small footprint — but only viable in certain places, high drilling costs, can trigger minor tremors.

front: Wave and tidal — advantages and disadvantages
back: Tides are entirely predictable with high energy density — but very high set-up cost, salt water corrosion and disturbed coastal habitats.
Lower running costs, protection from fuel price swings, lower product carbon footprint, and meeting legal and customer environmental targets.
Renewable sources produce power when conditions allow, not when it is needed.
Surplus electricity pumps water uphill; releasing it drives turbines when demand rises — used for national grid balancing.
Alkaline: cheap but single use. Rechargeable (NiMH, lithium-ion): higher initial cost but used hundreds of times, so cheaper and greener overall.

front: Why lithium-ion dominates phones and electric cars
back: It holds more energy for its weight.
No emissions at point of use, cheap to run, few moving parts — but slower to recharge, limited range and resource-intensive batteries.
A small engine plus battery and motor, recovering energy by regenerative braking — lower emissions without range anxiety, but more complex and heavier.

front: Mains vs battery vs solar in household products
back: Mains: constant high power but tied to a socket. Battery: portable and low voltage but limited capacity. Solar: no wiring but depends on light, usually paired with a rechargeable cell.
Using the wearer's movement to keep a watch or wearable charged.
